learn.title: Learn
learn.sub: Plain-language explanations of everything on these pages, written for someone who has just opened a BO account.
learn.what.b:
You tell it which companies on the Dhaka Stock Exchange you own or are watching. After each trading session it checks every one of them against a set of rules, and when something unusual happened it tells you, by email, Telegram or on these pages. It also shows what is true about each company right now, values your portfolio, and keeps score of how useful its own alerts were.

Everything runs on one computer that you or the person who set it up controls. Market data comes from the exchange's own website. Nothing about you is sent anywhere.
learn.not.b:
It never tells you to buy or sell. An alert is a fact, such as "BEXIMCO closed at its upper circuit, something it does about twice a year". What you do with that fact is your decision. It does not predict prices, and the historical numbers it shows describe the past, not the future.

It also does not place orders. You still trade through your broker's app.
learn.session.b: The DSE trades Sunday to Thursday. One trading day is a session. The close is the last price of the session, and every move on these pages is a change between closes: "1 session" compares today's close with yesterday's, "20 sessions" with the close about a month ago, "250 sessions" with about a year ago. Sessions, not calendar days, so holidays do not count.
learn.circuit.b:
The exchange limits how far a share can move in one day: 10% either way for shares under Tk 200, and smaller percentages for pricier shares. That limit is the circuit. A share that closes at its upper circuit rose as far as it was allowed to; at its lower circuit it fell as far as it could. Several sessions in a row at a circuit is rare and is worth knowing about, which is why there is a rule for it.

Two kinds of session have no limit, and the site does not count them as circuit hits: the first session after a record date, when the price is adjusted for the dividend, and sessions where the exchange lifts the limit and publishes a "Price Limit Open" notice. A move beyond the limit on any other day means a corporate action the site has no record of, so no alert is raised on it.
learn.category.t: Categories A, B, N and Z
learn.category.b: The exchange sorts companies by how they treat shareholders. A: paid a dividend of at least 10% and held its annual general meeting (AGM) on time. B: paid a smaller dividend. N: listed recently, not yet rated. Z: paid no dividend, or its AGM is overdue, or it has not operated for six months. Category Z shares also settle more slowly. The category is shown next to every trading code.
learn.volume.b: Volume is the number of shares that changed hands in a session. On its own the number means little, so these pages show it against the stock's own average over the previous 20 sessions: 2x means twice the usual. A big price move on unusually high volume involved many people; the same move on thin volume may not mean much.
learn.unusual.b:
A 5% move is an ordinary day for some shares and a remarkable one for others. So instead of a fixed number, every rule compares today with the stock's own history, which goes back to 2013 for most companies. A percentile is a position in that history: the 95th percentile of daily moves is a move bigger than 95% of all the days this stock has had. When a page says "beyond its 95th percentile", it means today was in the top 5% for this company.

The pages call these numbers the stock's baselines. You can see them on each symbol page.
learn.trend.b: A moving average smooths out daily noise: the 20-session average is the mean of the last 20 closes, the 50-session average the mean of the last 50. "Above both averages" means the price is higher than both, which people read as an upward trend; "below both" as a downward one; "between" as undecided. The chart on each symbol page draws both lines.
learn.range.b: The lowest and highest closes of the last year, with a marker for where today's price sits between them. 0% is the low, 100% the high. A share near its 52-week low has fallen a long way from where it was; near its high, it has risen. Neither says what happens next.
learn.pe.t: P/E, EPS, NAV and dividend yield
learn.pe.b:
EPS is earnings per share, the company's yearly profit divided by its number of shares. P/E is the price divided by EPS: how many years of current profit the price equals. A P/E of 8 is cheaper than 20 on this one measure, but a low P/E can also mean the market expects profits to fall. Compare with the sector median shown next to it rather than with an absolute number.

NAV per share is the company's assets minus its debts, per share. Price divided by NAV below 1 means the share trades for less than the book value of what the company owns. Dividend yield is the last dividend as a percentage of the price. These figures come from the company's page on the exchange's website and can be a year old.
learn.psi.b: Listed companies must tell the exchange about anything that could move the price: results, dividends, big contracts, board decisions, changes of ownership. These filings are called price-sensitive information. The app records every PSI for the companies you follow and raises an alert when one appears, because a sudden price move very often has a filing behind it.
learn.dividend.b: A dividend is part of the profit paid to shareholders, in cash or as extra shares. "10% cash" means Tk 1 per share of Tk 10 face value, not 10% of the price. The record date is the day the company checks who owns its shares; to receive the dividend you must own the share at the close of the session before it. The AGM is the yearly shareholders' meeting where the dividend is approved. The overview lists upcoming record dates for your symbols.
learn.columns.b: Hover over any underlined column heading to see the same explanation.
learn.rules.b: Each rule fires at most once per episode, and most compare today with the stock's own baselines, so they fire a few times a year per company rather than every other day. The Rules page shows how often each one fired in 14 years of history and what the price typically did afterwards.
learn.alerts.b:
Every trading day at 16:30, after the session closes, the app fetches the day's prices and filings, runs every rule on every symbol you follow, and sends you what fired. The same alerts appear on the Overview and Alerts pages. Each alert states what happened and the numbers behind it, and most mention how often that happens for that stock.

You can switch rules off or change their thresholds per symbol on the symbol page. "Check alerts now" on the overview runs the rules on the latest data without waiting for the daily run.
learn.scorecard.b: The scorecard looks back at every alert you were sent and records what the price did 5 and 20 sessions later, next to what the DSEX did over the same sessions and what the 14-year backtest expected. It grades the rules, not you. If a rule's alerts are usually followed by falls, that is useful to know when the next one arrives. An alert is pending until 20 sessions have passed.
learn.portfolio.b: Cost is what you paid: quantity times average cost from your broker's statement. Market value is quantity times today's close. Profit or loss is the difference, and it is unrealised: it only becomes real money when you sell, and it ignores brokerage and tax. Weight is each position's share of the whole. "Since statement" compares today's value with the value printed on the statement you imported.
learn.ai.b: When an AI provider is configured, a language model writes a short note from the alerts of the day. It only sees what the rules produced and the historical numbers; it is told to explain, never to advise, and not to invent anything. Treat it as a readable version of the alerts, and read the alerts themselves when a number matters.
home.title: Daily facts about Dhaka Stock Exchange shares, in plain words
home.lead: Add the stocks you own or follow. After every trading session the site checks them against fixed rules and tells you what happened: unusual volume, circuit hits, moves outside the stock's normal range, upcoming record dates. Facts only, never buy or sell advice.
home.privacy: Free and open source. Your account lives only on this server and is never sold or shared.
home.demo_note: The demo is a shared, read-only account with a sample watchlist and portfolio.
home.step1_b: Type a trading code such as GP or BATBC, or use Find stocks to screen the whole market by sector, price, P/E and more.
home.step2_b: After the 2:30 pm close the data is refreshed and each stock is checked against the rules. Every rule is explained on the Learn page, with how often it fires and what tended to follow.
home.step3_t: 3. Read the alert, in your language
home.step3_b: Alerts appear here and, if you want, by email or Telegram, in English or Bangla, with a short AI note that explains the terms. The scorecard later shows what happened after each alert.
home.f1: Overview of your stocks: close, moves over 1 and 20 sessions, volume against the usual, circuit hits and a 60-session sparkline.
home.f2: Portfolio value, profit or loss and weights from your broker statement, across several accounts.
home.f3: Market today: a sector board, the biggest moves and upcoming record dates.
home.f4: Find stocks: a screener over everything that traded, with presets for beginners.
home.f5: Learn: sessions, circuit breakers, categories, P/E, record dates and every column, explained for a first-time investor.

home.about_data: Prices, volumes, filings and dividend declarations come from the Dhaka Stock Exchange's public website, fetched once a day by this server, plus a public research archive for 2012 to 2026. Figures are derived statistics, not a redistribution of the exchange's feed.
home.about_privacy: What is stored: your email, a hashed password, your watchlist and any holdings you import. What leaves this server: alerts to the email or Telegram chat you confirm, and, when the AI note is on, the alert text (trading codes, prices and percentages, never your name, email or holdings) to the AI provider that writes it. No analytics, no advertising.
